intro: Patrizia Prati plays Chopin’s Nocturne in F♯ major, Op. 15 No. 2, in the empty rooms of the Museum of Romanticism in Madrid. In the middle of the piece, the opening melody takes a quick, murmuring form.

sections.label: A · Melody in F♯ major
sections.mNote: The melody moves above a left-hand accompaniment.

sections.label: B · Middle section, doppio movimento
sections.mNote: Dotted rhythms over a leaping bass, marked doppio movimento.

sections.label: C · Return of the opening melody
sections.mNote: A pause comes before the slow melody returns.

sections.label: D · Close in F♯ major
sections.mNote: Small notes descend above the final bass note.

cues.title: Upbeat and opening phrase
cues.text: Two quick notes, A♯ and B, form the upbeat to the melody. The phrase falls, rests on repeated C♯s, then rises in a flourish. Chopin keeps adding new short runs to the tune, which remains easy to recognise.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, upbeat and bars 1–16. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Museum of Romanticism recording, 2015
cues.text: Prati recorded at the Museum of Romanticism on 24 November 2015 without an audience, because coughing and mobile phones had ruined a first concert there. She gave the recordings, twelve Chopin nocturnes among them, to Wikimedia Spain.
cues.evidence: Rubén Ojeda (Wikimedia España), “La música del Romanticismo suena en Wikipedia”, 14 February 2016: https://diff.wikimedia.org/es/2016/02/14/la-musica-del-romanticismo-suena-en-wikipedia/ ; Commons file page: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fryderyk_Chopin_-_Nocturne_op._15_n.2_Fis-dur_-_Patrizia_Prati.ogg

cues.title: Middle section over C♯ bass
cues.text: The quick middle section, marked doppio movimento, begins in bar 25 over a C♯ bass. The right hand plays a dotted melody above a running accompaniment, both sotto voce. The bass makes wide leaps.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 25–32: C♯ dominant harmony, doppio movimento and sotto voce. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening theme
cues.text: The middle section ends in repeated figures that slow and die away. A pause separates them from the A♯–B upbeat, which returns. The melody comes back in the first tempo with new ornaments.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 47–52, marked molto rallentando, smorzando and a Tempo. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing flourishes in F♯ major
cues.text: The closing flourishes descend through the notes of F♯ major. The marking smorzando directs the piano to die away, and the final low F♯ comes at the bottom of the decoration.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 60–62. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
